records.story: The Overholt family farmed and distilled rye at West Overton, in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, from the early 1800s, and the brand dates itself to 1810, when Abraham Overholt (died 1870) took charge of the family still and made it a business. In 1859 the firm, as A. Overholt & Co., added a second distillery at Broad Ford. Abraham's grandson Henry Clay Frick (1849 to 1919), the industrialist born at West Overton, took control in 1881. The West Overton distillery closed with Prohibition and never reopened, but the firm held a federal permit to sell its whiskey as medicine. After repeal the label passed to National Distillers, which closed the Broad Ford still house in 1951, and the whiskey moved from distillery to distillery. In 1987 the James B. Beam Distilling Co. bought the brand with the National Distillers labels and settled its making in Kentucky. In 2020 the bottle rose from 80 to 86 proof without chill filtering, and in 2022 it gained a fourth year. Behind a bar it is the name that carries the Monongahela story, though the whiskey in it is Kentucky rye.

records.story: Sagamore Spirit takes its name from Sagamore Farm, a horse farm in Baltimore County, Maryland, whose limestone spring water brings the whiskey to strength, carried some twenty miles to the bottling hall. The founders set out to revive Maryland rye, a style the state had lost with Prohibition and one often described as softer than the Pennsylvania kind. While their own distillery was planned, they had two rye recipes distilled for them in Indiana, one high in rye and one lower, aged apart and then married and proofed in Maryland: that marriage became the Signature, at 83 proof. The distillery opened in April 2017 on the Port Covington waterfront in Baltimore, with a copper column still, and by the house's account it was the first in Maryland since Prohibition to distil, age and bottle rye. Its own Maryland spirit reached the bottle in stages, and in May 2024 the house launched Sagamore Small Batch Rye Whiskey, its first rye made wholly in Maryland, at 93 proof. Behind a bar the Signature is the bottle that put the Maryland rye name back in front of guests, and the one to set beside its newer stablemate.

records.story: Western Pennsylvania made rye for close to two centuries, as the house tells it, and the style took the name of the Monongahela valley. In 1791 Congress taxed whiskey, and the farmers and distillers of the region rose against the excise. The distillery's name recalls one of them, a man named Wigle who attacked a federal excise officer, was convicted of treason and condemned to hang, and was pardoned by George Washington (1732 to 1799) in November 1795. A Pittsburgh family opened Wigle to the public in the Strip District in March 2012, and it is generally counted the city's first distillery since Prohibition. From the start it milled, fermented and pot distilled regional grain itself, and its ryes carry wheat and malted barley beside the rye, with no corn. In 2022 the founding family agreed to sell Wigle and its sister cidery to Pittsburgh Spirits. Behind a bar Wigle is the name that shows what the western Pennsylvania rye tradition tastes like when it is made in the city again, from grain grown in the region.

records.story: Two friends founded Mountain Laurel Spirits in Bristol, Pennsylvania, on the Delaware above Philadelphia, in 2011, to make rye in the Pennsylvania manner again. One of them had grown up around rye at his family's bar, and the whiskey is named for his father, who wore fedora hats and drank rye whiskey. The recipe was worked out with Michigan State University's artisan distilling programme, and it follows the old Monongahela pattern of rye and malt with no corn: 80 per cent rye, 15 malted barley and 5 malted rye, fermented for about a week and distilled twice on a pot still with a side column. The classic rests at least six months in new charred quarter casks, small barrels that give the young spirit its oak quickly, and by 2012 it was in bottle at 90 proof and being written about in Philadelphia. Larger barrels followed for straight and bonded ryes. Behind a bar Dad's Hat is the bottle that shows how a rye of rye and malt alone tastes when young: floral, spicy and dry, a different animal from the corn-rounded ryes of Kentucky.

records.story: Washington County, south of Pittsburgh, was the farm country of the Whiskey Rebellion, where in 1794 protesters against the federal excise on whiskey raised liberty poles as their banner. A family founded Liberty Pole Spirits in the town of Washington in July 2016, naming it for those poles and distilling small batches of whiskey in pot stills downtown. In 2023 the house moved to a larger campus in North Strabane, raising a liberty pole on the site in place of a groundbreaking, and Mingo Creek Craft Distillers, the company behind the label, moved all its work there. In May 2024 it released Old Monongahela Full Proof Rye, built on the old regional pattern: a mash high in rye, with malted rye, wheat and malted barley and not a kernel of corn, sweet mashed, batch distilled and filled at a low barrel entry proof of 108, then bottled at that same strength. Behind a bar it is the bottle that puts the style's own name on the label, and a way to show a guest what Monongahela rye meant before the corn of Kentucky's ryes became the habit.
